food_summary: The bacteria historically grouped as Lactobacillus include many specialists in fermented foods. Yoghurt commonly uses L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus; vegetable ferments contain other lactic acid bacteria suited to plant sugars, salt and progressively acidic conditions.

Their production of lactic acid changes flavour, preservation and texture. Different foods select different communities: the organisms growing in milk, kefir grains and cabbage brine are connected through fermentation chemistry, while living in distinct food habitats.
Leuconostoc bacteria participate in vegetable fermentations, producing organic acids and gas from plant carbohydrates. Their activity changes the environment available to the organisms that follow.

Kimchi studies track these community changes alongside acidity and metabolites. Ingredients, storage and the microbial starting population help explain why fermentation follows different paths in different batches.

Food-grade Rhizopus cultures grow branching filaments through cooked soybeans. These filaments bind the beans into tempeh, while fungal enzymes change components of the substrate and develop its texture and flavour.

This is a solid-state fermentation with access to oxygen. Starter experiments show that culture preparation affects performance. Tempeh is commonly cooked before eating: the meal delivers a transformed food whose nutritional value does not depend on the fungus establishing itself in the intestine.
Aspergillus oryzae is a koji mould grown on cooked grain. Its branching hyphae enter the substrate and produce enzymes that break starches and proteins into smaller molecules.

When koji is mixed with cooked soybeans and salt, its enzymes continue to help transform the paste. Salt-tolerant bacteria and yeasts participate in later miso maturation. The mould’s enzyme-making phase and the subsequent paste fermentation are distinct parts of the process.
Zygosaccharomyces includes yeasts adapted to demanding food environments. Members occur in traditional miso communities alongside bacteria and filamentous fungi.

A metagenomic study comparing koji-based and spontaneous misos found differences in their dominant fungi while also detecting yeast and bacterial genera typical of miso. Those communities connect food tradition with measurable microbial ecology.
Tetragenococcus bacteria occur in salty fermented-food communities, including miso. Their metabolism contributes to the changing chemistry of a paste during maturation.

The miso comparison linked here examined microbial composition across different production traditions. The food environment, its salt and its available substrates help organise which organisms grow together.
These acetic-acid bacteria use oxygen to convert ethanol into organic acids. Some species weave the cellulose sheet at the surface of kombucha.
Acetobacter oxidises ethanol to acetic acid where oxygen is available. Its activity helps shape the sourness of several mixed-culture drinks.
Meals create recurring changes in nutrient supply, hormone signals and intestinal activity. Fasting studies change the duration or placement of these feeding periods.

Streptococcus thermophilus is one of the two traditional yoghurt starter bacteria. In warm milk it ferments lactose and produces lactic acid. Together with Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, it helps turn liquid milk into an acidic protein gel.

The partnership changes the nutrients available to each bacterium during culturing. Cooling slows their activity. When live-culture yoghurt is eaten, microbial enzymes can also participate in lactose digestion.

Saccharomyces yeasts use sugars and can produce carbon dioxide and ethanol during fermentation. In bread starters they live alongside acid-producing bacteria; in kefir they participate in a different community carried by the grains.

Studies of sourdough connect yeast–bacterial interactions with aroma and dough rise. Baking kills most starter organisms, leaving their transformations in the loaf. Live fermented drinks and baked foods therefore deliver different microbial products and living populations.

living-well.title: Living well
living-well.intro: Food, movement and the microbial life of everyday health.

stories.title: Feed a community
stories.lead: Different fibres open different microbial pathways.

steps.label: A food reaches the colon
steps.text: Beans, oats, vegetables and whole grains supply carbohydrates that escape digestion in the small intestine. The structure of a fibre shapes which microbes can start breaking it down.

steps.label: Specialists open the structure
steps.text: Ruminococcus bromii can attach to resistant starch and begin dismantling it. Other organisms gain access to released sugars, making starch degradation a shared activity.

steps.label: Neighbours exchange metabolites
steps.text: The tested bifidobacterial and faecalibacterial strains produced more butyrate together than in the relevant monocultures. These are laboratory findings from defined strains.

steps.label: The lining receives fuel
steps.text: Butyrate is an important fuel for cells lining the colon. Its effects on metabolism and immune signalling connect microbial fermentation to the tissue that houses it.

stories.practical: Build meals around several fibre sources: pulses, whole grains, vegetables, nuts and seeds. Add variety gradually if a large change produces gas. The high-fibre arm of the Stanford diet trial increased microbial carbohydrate-processing capacity without increasing diversity across the whole group.

stories.title: Food already transformed
stories.lead: Microbes change food before it reaches you.

steps.label: Choose a fermentation
steps.text: Yoghurt, cabbage ferments and tempeh begin with different ingredients and communities. Their fermentation changes acidity, texture and food chemistry.

steps.label: A dietary experiment
steps.text: In a randomised study of 36 healthy adults, the fermented-food arm increased gut microbial diversity and reduced several inflammatory markers. Participants ate a mixture of foods.

steps.label: Follow the transformation
steps.text: Live-culture yoghurt, a baked loaf and cooked tempeh deliver different mixtures of living microbes, microbial products and transformed ingredients. Fermentation continues to matter after organisms are killed by cooking.

stories.practical: Try a food you enjoy as part of a meal: plain live-culture yoghurt with oats, tempeh with vegetables, or sauerkraut alongside beans. Open Fermentation sciences to see how each food is made.

stories.title: Move the ecosystem
stories.lead: Exercise changes the host that microbes live in.

steps.label: The host changes
steps.text: Movement changes circulation, energy use and intestinal physiology. Exercise studies measure how the microbial community responds alongside the person.

steps.label: A six-week experiment
steps.text: Previously sedentary adults completed supervised endurance training. Short-chain fatty acids increased in lean participants, with a different response in participants with obesity.

steps.label: Compare another result
steps.text: A separate three-week interval-training study found better fitness without a detectable change in bacterial composition. Duration, activity and the initial community help define the question.

stories.practical: Choose movement you can sustain and enjoy. The six-week study progressed from 30 to 60 minutes per session, three times weekly; it describes the experiment rather than a universal training prescription.

stories.title: A daily rhythm
stories.lead: Sleep changes the conditions of microbial life.

steps.label: Compare two nights
steps.text: Researchers compared adequate sleep with severe restriction while controlling diet and activity in healthy young men. This makes sleep itself an experimental variable.

steps.label: Count what changed
steps.text: After three restricted nights, microbial richness fell, while other diversity measures and intestinal permeability were unchanged. The gut responds along several distinct dimensions.

stories.practical: Keep a regular opportunity for sleep and notice the relationship between meal timing, digestion and how rested you feel. The experiment used an extreme two-hour sleep condition; it did not test a sleep supplement or a food cure.

stories.title: Signals and experience
stories.lead: Microbes participate in the body’s chemical conversation.

steps.label: A route to the brain
steps.text: The gut and brain exchange information through sensory nerves, circulating precursors, immune responses and microbial metabolites. Serotonin can activate a gut sensory fibre whose electrical signal travels toward the brainstem. Human studies then ask how particular changes relate to mood, stress and quality of life.

steps.label: Test a named strain
steps.text: In a small study of healthy volunteers, Bifidobacterium longum 1714 was associated with reduced stress responses and subtle memory changes. The study followed one strain through defined measurements.

stories.practical: Food, sleep, movement and social life offer everyday ways to support how you feel. The research links here let you inspect a microbial intervention directly: participants, preparation, measurements and results.

stories.title: Make room for digestion
stories.lead: Transit shapes the ecosystem as food moves through it.

steps.label: Time changes the substrate
steps.text: As gut contents move, nutrients are used up and microbial products accumulate. Transit time helps determine the environment encountered by successive communities.

steps.label: Observe the pattern
steps.text: A study connecting colonic transit with microbial metabolism found that time in the colon was related to the balance of fermentation and protein breakdown. Stool measurements are part of that moving system.

stories.practical: Notice patterns over several days: meal composition, fluid intake, movement and stool consistency. For persistent constipation or diarrhoea, the Illness & recovery page connects symptoms to mechanisms and research.

stories.title: Resistant starch
stories.lead: Some starch feeds microbes after escaping our own digestion.

steps.label: Structure matters
steps.text: Starch digestibility depends on its plant structure and preparation. Resistant fractions reach the colon, where specialist organisms can attach to and break apart the starch granules.

steps.label: A keystone opens a resource
steps.text: In laboratory communities, Ruminococcus bromii unlocks resistant starch for other bacteria. Its activity changes who can use the food and which fermentation products become available.

steps.label: Partners share the products
steps.text: Released carbohydrates support other fermenters. Acetate and lactate can then feed butyrate producers, connecting the initial starch degraders to the wider community.

stories.practical: Try beans, lentils, oats and other whole grains as ordinary meal ingredients. Different resistant starches feed different communities; introduce larger portions gradually if they cause gas.

stories.title: Beans, lentils & chickpeas
stories.lead: A meal can deliver protein and microbial food together.

steps.label: Two destinations
steps.text: Pulses contain protein, starch and fermentable carbohydrates. Our enzymes digest part of the meal; the remaining carbohydrates supply organisms further down the gut.

steps.label: A shared fermentation
steps.text: Bifidobacteria ferment carbohydrates into products including acetate and lactate. Other bacteria can use these products, extending the food web beyond the first consumer.

steps.label: A regular place at the table
steps.text: The Stanford diet intervention tracked changes over weeks. Increasing fibre changed microbial carbohydrate-processing capacity; microbial diversity did not rise across the entire high-fibre group.

stories.practical: Add a small serving of cooked beans or lentils to soups, salads and grain dishes. Increase portions as your digestion adapts. Cook dried beans thoroughly; canned beans are a convenient starting point.

stories.title: Oats, fruit & live yoghurt
stories.lead: Combine a plant substrate with a food transformed by microbes.

steps.label: The plant part
steps.text: Oats and fruit contribute a mixture of fibres. Microbes differ in their ability to use these structures, so a mixed meal offers more than a single purified substrate.

steps.label: The cultured part
steps.text: Yoghurt cultures ferment milk before it reaches the gut. Their lactase activity can improve digestion of the yoghurt’s lactose in people who digest lactose poorly.

steps.label: The whole meal
steps.text: The fermented-food arm of the Stanford trial increased microbial diversity and reduced several inflammatory markers. Participants ate a range of fermented foods, so the result describes that dietary pattern.

stories.practical: Pair plain live-culture yoghurt with oats and fruit. Use lactose-free yoghurt if it suits your digestion. Choose a portion and combination you enjoy enough to eat regularly.

stories.title: Care for the mouth’s ecosystem
stories.lead: Repeated sugar exposure reshapes a microbial habitat before food reaches the stomach.

steps.label: A surface community
steps.text: Dental plaque is an attached microbial community. Food, saliva and the tooth surface create local environments that differ from the surrounding mouth.

steps.label: Frequent sugar changes the chemistry
steps.text: Sugar fermentation lowers plaque pH. Repeated acid exposure favours acid-tolerant organisms and removes minerals from tooth enamel.

steps.label: Change the daily environment
steps.text: Cleaning plaque, using fluoride toothpaste and reducing frequent sugary snacks change the conditions in which the oral community lives. The goal is a stable tooth-supporting habitat.

stories.practical: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth and keep sugary foods and drinks to mealtimes. A dental professional can help with bleeding gums, persistent pain or dry mouth.

stories.title: Fasting
stories.lead: Intermittent fasting, Ramadan, ketosis and the importance of timing, nutrition and life stage.

steps.label: Different fasts, different lives
steps.text: Ramadan daylight fasting includes abstaining from fluids, with eating after sunset and before dawn. Daily eating windows and alternate-day schedules use different rules. Ramadan stool studies report community shifts, but food, sleep and energy intake also change. Those observations cannot isolate a timing effect.

steps.label: What intermittent fasting achieves
steps.text: Across randomised trials, intermittent fasting generally produces metabolic and weight outcomes similar to continuous energy restriction. A 12-month trial found no significant extra benefit from an early eating window when both groups restricted calories. A separate programme combining fasting and protein pacing changed microbial profiles, but cannot isolate fasting from the protein intervention.

steps.label: Timing can matter without weight loss
steps.text: A small controlled-feeding crossover experiment in men with prediabetes found improved insulin sensitivity with early eating despite weight maintenance. This is evidence about a specific protocol and population. Other timing trials measure different outcomes, including stool communities; a metabolic improvement does not automatically imply a microbiome change.

steps.label: From stored carbohydrate to ketones
steps.text: As liver glycogen declines, the body relies more on fat and can produce more ketone bodies. There is no universal hour when everyone enters ketosis: food composition, activity and metabolic state matter. A ketogenic diet, fasting and taking a ketone supplement are distinct interventions.

steps.label: Ketosis and the microbial community
steps.text: Ketogenic feeding changed stool communities in a human inpatient study. Follow-up cultures and mouse experiments tested ketone effects on bifidobacteria and intestinal immune cells. This offers a mechanism to investigate; it does not show that fasting-induced ketosis treats human gut inflammation.

steps.label: Women: hormones and life stage
steps.text: In a small eight-week analysis in women with obesity, several measured sex hormones remained stable while DHEA decreased. Men were excluded, and menstrual-cycle ovarian hormones were not assessed before menopause. The study cannot establish fertility effects, long-term safety or an optimal fasting window for women.

steps.label: Women and men: what is still uncertain
steps.text: Direct comparisons between women and men remain scarce. Menstrual status, menopause, training load and adequate energy intake may influence responses. Current evidence does not justify fixed fasting hours by sex or menstrual phase. Male-only results and short female-only studies should both be read within their limits.

stories.practical: Choose a schedule that preserves nourishing meals, protein, fibre and a workable social life. More fasting or more ketones is not an established goal for better gut health. During Ramadan, plan hydration within permitted hours. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, eating-disorder history, disrupted menstrual cycles and glucose-lowering medicines warrant individual clinical advice before fasting. Unplanned weight loss, persistent fatigue or menstrual changes are reasons to reassess the plan.

stories.title: Daily eating windows
stories.lead: Early, late and self-selected schedules put timing to a direct test.

steps.label: Timing and food are separate levers
steps.text: A controlled feeding trial varied carbohydrate content and daily eating windows within calorie restriction. It tracked body composition together with microbial and metabolite measurements.

steps.label: Early and late windows
steps.text: In a three-month trial, early and late windows produced different changes in diversity measures and some bacterial genera. Overall between-group community differences were not significant.

steps.label: What happens over twelve weeks?
steps.text: A larger multicentre trial compared early, late and self-selected windows with Mediterranean-diet education alone. The extra time restriction did not produce a significant between-group difference in liver outcomes or measured stool microbiota.

stories.practical: Start by noticing when you eat, how you sleep and how you feel between meals. An overnight interval and an earlier final meal are different choices from a multi-day fast. Preserve nourishing meals and adequate protein. Pregnancy, breastfeeding, a history of eating disorders and glucose-lowering medicines change the clinical decision; discuss a fasting plan with your clinician in these circumstances.

stories.title: Longer fasts & refeeding
stories.lead: Clinical fasting studies follow what happens during the fast and after food returns.

steps.label: Fasting followed by a diet programme
steps.text: A trial substudy compared a five-day fast followed by modified DASH eating with the diet alone. Blood pressure, medication need and body-mass index were lower in the fasting programme at three months.

steps.label: Microbial pathways
steps.text: The same substudy measured changes in taxa and gene modules linked to short-chain-fatty-acid production. These exploratory measurements connect the clinical result to possible biological routes.

steps.label: From mechanism to human trials
steps.text: A mouse experiment transferred microbes from fasting donors and reduced autoimmune disease in recipients. Its accompanying human pilot measured microbial and blood changes. These are distinct steps toward testing a treatment.

stories.practical: The five-day intervention described here was part of a structured clinical programme with refeeding and medication assessment. Use that study to understand the biology; planning a prolonged fast requires clinical supervision, especially with blood-pressure or glucose-lowering medicines.

stories.title: Passing stool & cleaning afterwards
stories.lead: Posture, gentle anal care and the cultural life of the toilet.

steps.label: Find a comfortable position
steps.text: Supporting the feet and leaning forward can make bowel emptying feel easier. In healthy volunteers, squatting reduced reported effort; in a constipation clinic, footstools did not improve a simulated evacuation test. Comfort, mobility and pelvic-floor function matter more than a single supposedly perfect posture.

steps.label: Clean the outside gently
steps.text: After passing stool, clean around the anus with gentle wiping, water or both, then pat dry. Avoid repeated scrubbing, strong fragrances and very hot water. This is care of the external skin: routine cleaning does not require flushing water into the rectum. Rectal irrigation for a bowel condition is a separate treatment taught by a clinician.

steps.label: Water, privacy and cultural practice
steps.text: Qualitative research in coastal Odisha found that water-based cleansing, privacy and daily routines shaped whether people used a toilet. A SuSanA practitioner survey describes variation across countries and between public, private, rural and urban settings. It is an exploratory account, not a representative map of religions or national habits.

steps.label: Bidets: a tool with a context
steps.text: A Japanese convenience-sample survey documented electric-bidet habits and associations between some washing behaviours and itching. People may wash more because they already have symptoms, so the association does not establish cause. Water access, device design and mobility shape what feels practical; gentle cleaning is the aim.

stories.practical: Use a stable foot support if comfortable, keep your feet supported and avoid prolonged straining. Choose gentle external cleaning and dry without rubbing. Do not climb onto a seated toilet to squat. Persistent pain, bleeding, leakage or difficulty emptying deserves assessment rather than progressively stronger cleaning. Wash hands with soap after toilet use.

stories.title: Slow cooking & slow eating
stories.lead: What time changes in the pot, in the mouth and during a meal.

steps.label: Give ingredients time to soften
steps.text: Stews and braises can make beans, vegetables and tougher cuts easier to prepare and chew. The digestive effect depends on the ingredient and its structure, not simply the clock. A small bean-meal experiment found different glucose responses after home boiling and commercial canning; it did not test a slow cooker.

steps.label: Food structure matters
steps.text: After a cooked white-bean meal, some starch reached the end of the small intestine enclosed within plant cell walls. This helps explain why a cooked pulse can still feed colonic microbes. Longer cooking can also increase starch accessibility: slower cooking does not automatically mean slower digestion or more resistant starch.

steps.label: Give the meal some time
steps.text: Experiments that slowed eating generally reduced intake during that meal, without reliably changing later hunger. Chewing comfortably and pausing between bites may help you notice the meal and your appetite. These findings do not establish lasting weight loss, better nutrient absorption or a direct microbiome benefit.

steps.label: Make slowness practical and safe
steps.text: Try an unhurried meal and cook to a safe temperature rather than chasing a fixed number of hours. Slow-cooker safety depends on handling and heating. Raw dried kidney beans need proper soaking and high-temperature boiling; a low-temperature slow cooker alone may leave lectins active. Canned beans are a convenient already-cooked option.

stories.practical: Choose a stew or other meal you enjoy and leave enough time to eat comfortably. Take manageable bites, chew to a comfortable texture and pause if useful; there is no evidence-based chew count for everyone. Keep adequate nourishment as the goal. Follow appliance and food-safety instructions, especially for meat and dried kidney beans.

fermentation.title: Fermentation sciences
fermentation.intro: Watch a community turn ingredients into food.

stories.title: Yoghurt
stories.lead: A partnership that turns milk into a soft gel.

steps.label: Milk & culture
steps.text: Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus grow together in milk. Each changes the conditions and nutrients available to its partner.

steps.label: Lactose becomes acid
steps.text: The bacteria ferment lactose to lactic acid. As acidity rises, milk proteins assemble into a gel that traps water.

steps.label: Cool the finished food
steps.text: Cooling slows further fermentation. Refrigerated live-culture yoghurt contains the transformed milk and its starter organisms. Heating after fermentation changes that living population.

steps.label: From food to gut
steps.text: Microbial lactase in yoghurt helps digest its lactose. Fermented milk is one of the foods included in human diet interventions, where the whole dietary pattern is measured.

stories.practical: Serve plain yoghurt with oats or fruit, or use it in a savoury dressing. For preparation, the WSU method specifies milk heating, starter temperature and incubation; its linked procedure includes storage instructions. Keep finished yoghurt refrigerated.
stories.oxygen: Starter cultures work in the milk; no aeration step is needed.
controls: Warmth supports these thermophilic starter organisms; refrigeration slows them.
Longer culturing changes acidity and firmness. Stop according to the tested method.

stories.title: Sauerkraut
stories.lead: A succession of bacteria under the brine.

steps.label: Salt draws a brine
steps.text: Salt draws liquid from shredded cabbage. Keeping the cabbage beneath its brine creates conditions favouring lactic acid bacteria.

steps.label: Early fermentation
steps.text: Leuconostoc and other lactic acid bacteria use cabbage sugars. Acid and gas change the vessel, and the community shifts as the environment becomes more acidic.

steps.label: A sour community
steps.text: Acid-tolerant bacteria continue the transformation. Temperature affects its pace: the USDA method gives about three to four weeks at 21–24°C.

steps.label: A food at the table
steps.text: Refrigeration slows microbial activity. Canning heats the finished food, preserving the acidified cabbage while reducing its living microbial population.

stories.practical: Use the linked USDA recipe for cabbage, salt, brine coverage and storage. Its warm fermentation range is 21–24°C; cooler conditions take longer. Keep fully fermented kraut refrigerated, or follow the specified canning procedure. Serve as a condiment alongside a meal.
controls: The USDA method gives 3–4 weeks at 21–24°C and 5–6 weeks at 16–18°C.
Salt draws the brine and shapes the community. Use the proportions in the tested procedure.

stories.title: Tempeh
stories.lead: A fungus weaves beans into a food.

steps.label: Prepare the substrate
steps.text: Cooked soybeans provide a moist, nutrient-rich surface for a Rhizopus starter. This is a solid-state fermentation.

steps.label: Hyphae connect the beans
steps.text: Rhizopus grows branching filaments between the beans. The growing mycelium binds them into a coherent cake.

steps.label: Enzymes change the food
steps.text: Fungal enzymes break down components of the beans, changing texture, flavour and nutrient accessibility. Starter and substrate both shape the result.

steps.label: Cook & eat
steps.text: Tempeh is commonly cooked before eating. The meal delivers a transformed protein-rich food; its value does not depend on the fungus remaining alive in the gut.

stories.practical: Cook tempeh according to the producer’s instructions and store it as directed. Pair it with vegetables and a grain or pulse. The process shown here explains fungal fermentation; the source paper describes laboratory starter experiments.
stories.oxygen: Rhizopus needs access to oxygen while it grows.
controls: The mycelium grows on a solid substrate with access to air.
A food-grade Rhizopus starter defines the intended fungus.

stories.title: Kefir
stories.lead: A grain carries a community of bacteria and yeasts.

steps.label: A living grain
steps.text: Kefir grains carry bacteria and yeasts in a shared matrix. Adding them to milk introduces a mixed community.

steps.label: A microbial succession
steps.text: Different members grow and exchange metabolites over the course of fermentation. Their activity produces acids, gas and flavour compounds.

steps.label: Strain & cool
steps.text: Removing the grains separates the reusable culture from the fermented drink. Cooling slows subsequent activity.

steps.label: Drink & digest
steps.text: The finished food combines fermented milk, microbial products and living organisms. Grain composition explains some differences between batches.

stories.practical: Keep commercial kefir refrigerated as directed and use it with a meal or as a base for oats. A mixed culture produces a different food from yoghurt.
stories.oxygen: Conditions depend on the food and culture.

stories.title: Kimchi
stories.lead: Vegetables become a changing acidic habitat.

steps.label: The ingredients
steps.text: Vegetables supply carbohydrates and their surface communities; salt and seasonings shape the starting conditions.

steps.label: Bacteria ferment sugars
steps.text: Lactic acid bacteria produce organic acids and other flavour compounds as the vegetables ferment.

steps.label: A changing food
steps.text: Storage temperature and time change the balance of organisms and the sourness of the food.

steps.label: Serve a portion
steps.text: Kimchi is one of several fermented vegetables included in human dietary intervention research.

stories.practical: Use a refrigerated product or a tested recipe for the specific vegetables you are preparing. Serve a small portion beside a meal; salt content differs across products.
stories.oxygen: Conditions depend on the food and culture.

stories.title: Sourdough
stories.lead: Bacteria and yeasts raise a dough together.

steps.label: Feed the starter
steps.text: Flour and water supply nutrients to a community of yeasts and bacteria. Refreshing it provides another supply of substrate.

steps.label: Gas & acid
steps.text: Yeasts and some bacteria generate gas; lactic acid bacteria acidify the dough. The community changes flavour and structure.

steps.label: Bake the dough
steps.text: Heat sets the loaf and kills most starter organisms. The transformed grain and fermentation products remain part of the food.

steps.label: Bread as food
steps.text: A baked sourdough loaf contributes to a meal through its ingredients and fermentation history. Whole-grain content changes its fibre contribution.

stories.practical: Choose bread for its ingredients and how it fits your meals. Baking transforms the starter into food; a sourdough label alone does not describe the whole-grain or fibre content.
stories.oxygen: Conditions depend on the food and culture.

stories.title: Miso
stories.lead: Koji enzymes and a salt-tolerant community transform a paste.

steps.label: Make koji
steps.text: Aspergillus oryzae grows on cooked grain and produces enzymes that break larger food molecules into smaller ones.

steps.label: Combine with beans
steps.text: Koji enzymes act in the soybean mixture, releasing sugars and amino acids.

steps.label: Mature the paste
steps.text: Salt-tolerant yeasts and bacteria join ongoing enzyme activity during maturation. A study of spontaneous nesashi miso found a different fungal community, led by Mucor, from the koji-based misos used for comparison.

steps.label: Season a meal
steps.text: Miso adds fermented flavour in a concentrated salty ingredient. Heating changes the living population while preserving much of the food’s flavour.

stories.practical: Use miso as a seasoning in soup, sauces or dressings. Follow the product’s storage directions and account for its salt alongside the rest of the meal.
stories.oxygen: Conditions depend on the food and culture.

stories.title: Kombucha
stories.lead: Tea transformed by a partnership of yeasts and acetic-acid bacteria.

steps.label: Tea meets a living starter
steps.text: Yeasts split sugar and produce ethanol and carbon dioxide. Acetic-acid bacteria use that ethanol near the oxygen-rich surface. The floating cellulose layer houses part of the community; the starter liquid also carries living organisms.

steps.label: A sour, living drink
steps.text: As fermentation proceeds, organic acids accumulate and sweetness changes. The University of Georgia method uses a breathable cover and a measured starter acidity. Time alone does not describe the state of a ferment.

steps.label: Chill and taste
steps.text: Refrigeration slows the community. Sugar, caffeine, alcohol and acids remain in amounts that vary between batches. Enjoy kombucha as a fermented drink; its composition is a separate question from whether it changes a particular health outcome.

stories.practical: Use the complete linked University of Georgia procedure, including its starter-pH check, sanitation and refrigeration instructions. Use a food-grade starter. Discard a mouldy batch. Sealed bottles can build dangerous pressure; follow the procedure’s storage guidance.

stories.title: Water kefir
stories.lead: A dairy-free fermentation held together by living grains.

steps.label: Grains carry the community
steps.text: Water-kefir grains contain bacteria and yeasts embedded in a polysaccharide matrix. They are a different culture from milk-kefir grains and grow in a sugar-water medium.

steps.label: Sugar feeds several partners
steps.text: Lactic-acid bacteria, yeasts and acetic-acid bacteria share the available substrates. Their products include organic acids, carbon dioxide and ethanol. Culture and conditions shape the finished drink.

steps.label: Strain, chill, reuse
steps.text: Straining separates the grains from the drink so the culture can start another batch. The liquid remains biologically active, and its residual sugar and alcohol vary.

stories.practical: Buy water-kefir grains from a food-culture supplier and follow that culture’s water, sugar, temperature and storage instructions. The linked CSU guide explains the difference between milk and water kefir; its recipe is for milk kefir. Refrigerate the finished drink and manage bottle pressure.

stories.title: Fermented dill pickles
stories.lead: Cucumbers become sour through microbial fermentation.

steps.label: Begin with the brine
steps.text: The USDA procedure combines pickling cucumbers, salt, water, dill and a measured amount of vinegar. The proportions establish the starting environment for fermentation.

steps.label: Acid accumulates
steps.text: Lactic-acid bacteria consume vegetable sugars while the cucumbers remain submerged. Acidity increases, flavour develops and the brine becomes cloudy.

steps.label: Keep the crunch
steps.text: Refrigeration slows fermentation. Heat processing creates a different stored product and reduces the living microbial population. The food still contains the acids and transformed vegetable tissue.

stories.practical: Follow the complete USDA recipe linked here, including its vinegar and salt quantities, temperature range and spoilage checks. Keep the vegetables under the brine and refrigerate as instructed. Do not improvise a reduced-salt version of a preservation recipe.

stories.title: Fermented carrots
stories.lead: A simple vegetable ferment with a sweet starting material.

steps.label: Prepare the vegetables
steps.text: Carrot sticks supply sugars and a firm plant structure. A wet brine surrounds the pieces; a food-safe weight keeps them beneath the surface.

steps.label: A changing community
steps.text: Vegetable-associated lactic-acid bacteria ferment available sugars. As acids accumulate, the environment favours organisms that tolerate sour conditions. Salt, temperature and submersion shape the process.

steps.label: Serve with a meal
steps.text: The finished carrots bring acidity, texture and plant fibre to the plate. A small serving can accompany beans, grains or sandwiches. Refrigeration slows further change.

stories.practical: Use the University of Minnesota wet-brine vegetable method linked here, including its salt calculation, equipment, temperature and storage guidance. Keep carrots submerged. Discard spoiled or mouldy batches.

illness-recovery.title: Infections
illness-recovery.intro: Gut pathogens, oral biofilms and the mechanisms of infection and recovery.

stories.title: H. pylori
stories.lead: A bacterium makes a home in stomach mucus.

steps.label: Arrival
steps.text: Helicobacter pylori reaches the stomach and establishes a long-lived association with the gastric lining. In many people infection persists for years.

steps.label: Move through mucus
steps.text: Local changes in acidity alter the properties of gastric mucus. Experiments show H. pylori using this change to move through a material that otherwise restricts its movement.

steps.label: Urease chemistry
steps.text: A gated urea channel supplies substrate to urease. Urea is converted into ammonia and carbon dioxide, helping the bacterium manage its acidic surroundings.

steps.label: Host response
steps.text: Persistent infection drives inflammation in the stomach lining. Long-term eradication studies examine outcomes including gastric cancer, linking microbial persistence to disease prevention.

steps.label: Testing & treatment
steps.text: Breath testing and stool antigen testing detect active infection. The 2024 ACG adult guideline recommends bismuth quadruple therapy when susceptibility is unknown and advises against empiric clarithromycin triple therapy. Local resistance and prior antibiotics shape the regimen.

steps.label: Confirm clearance
steps.text: The ACG guideline calls for a test of cure at least four weeks after antibiotics, with acid-suppressing PPIs held for two weeks to reduce false negatives. Arrange the timing with the treating clinician.

stories.practical: Treatment targets a persistent infection and is followed by confirmation of clearance. The linked ACG source concerns adults in North America and was published in 2024; treatment selection depends on resistance, allergies and prior antibiotic exposure.

stories.title: C. difficile
stories.lead: A disturbed community loses some of its protection.

steps.label: A community is disrupted
steps.text: Antibiotic exposure can reduce competitors and change the resources and bile-acid environment in which C. difficile grows. Spores allow it to persist outside the body.

steps.label: Toxins damage tissue
steps.text: Toxigenic C. difficile produces toxins A and B. Infection can inflame the colon and cause diarrhoea, fever and abdominal pain. A positive test without symptoms can instead represent colonisation.

steps.label: Treat the infection
steps.text: CDC describes oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin for confirmed infection. Testing is interpreted alongside diarrhoea and other clinical findings. Unnecessary repeat testing after symptoms resolve can remain positive.

steps.label: Restore protection
steps.text: A randomised trial of an oral purified spore preparation reduced recurrence after standard antibiotics in adults with recurrent infection. This asks a different question from adding a supermarket probiotic.

stories.practical: New diarrhoea during or after antibiotics deserves clinical assessment, especially with fever or abdominal pain. Recurrent C. difficile has specific microbiome-based treatment options. Their indications and delivery differ from fermented foods.

stories.title: Norovirus
stories.lead: A human-cell virus in the intestinal ecosystem.

steps.label: Exposure
steps.text: Norovirus spreads through contaminated food, water, surfaces and close contact. It infects people; gut bacteriophages infect bacteria.

steps.label: Infect the intestinal cells
steps.text: Human intestinal enteroid experiments let researchers grow norovirus in tissue derived from human intestinal cells and examine host factors and viral replication.

steps.label: Fluid loss
steps.text: Vomiting and diarrhoea can rapidly deplete fluid and salts. Oral rehydration replaces these losses; severe dehydration needs medical care.

steps.label: Recovery & transmission
steps.text: Most illness resolves in one to three days. Viral shedding can continue after symptoms stop. CDC advises staying home for 48 hours after symptoms end, plus careful handwashing and cleaning.

stories.practical: Use oral rehydration fluids to replace losses. Decreased urination, marked dizziness or unusual drowsiness can signal dehydration. Antibiotics do not treat norovirus. The studies examine human intestinal tissue models.

stories.title: Giardia
stories.lead: A protist attaches to the small-intestinal surface.

steps.label: Cysts arrive
steps.text: Giardia cysts reach the gut through contaminated water, food or contact. The organism’s active form lives in the small intestine.

steps.label: Attachment & digestion
steps.text: Trophozoites attach at the intestinal surface. Infection can interfere with absorption and lead to diarrhoea, gas and bloating.

steps.label: Testing & treatment
steps.text: Stool testing identifies the parasite. CDC lists tinidazole, nitazoxanide and metronidazole among effective medicines; hydration remains important during diarrhoea.

steps.label: After the infection
steps.text: Some people continue to have symptoms after Giardia has cleared. Follow-up of an outbreak found increased rates of IBS and fatigue years later. Repeat symptoms deserve assessment rather than automatic retreatment.

stories.practical: Persistent symptoms can reflect continuing infection, reinfection or changes after clearance. CDC’s approach distinguishes these possibilities with repeat stool assessment when appropriate. Treatment choice depends on the patient and local availability.

stories.title: After antibiotics
stories.lead: Recovery is an ecological process.

steps.label: A broad disturbance
steps.text: Antibiotics change microbial populations beyond the organism targeted by treatment. The starting community and antibiotic exposure shape what follows.

steps.label: Reoccupation
steps.text: Surviving organisms grow into available niches. Introduced organisms interact with those survivors, so adding a preparation can change the recovery path.

steps.label: Compare recovery routes
steps.text: In one human experiment, an 11-strain probiotic delayed return of the native mucosal community; autologous stool transfer accelerated it. The study measured community reconstitution after a specific antibiotic exposure.

steps.label: Return to everyday function
steps.text: Eating and digestion are the practical context for recovery. Fermented foods are foods, while microbiome therapies for recurrent infection are clinical interventions with their own evidence.

stories.practical: Use antibiotics as prescribed and discuss new or persistent diarrhoea with the prescriber. Resume a varied diet as tolerated. The recovery experiment does not establish a universal probiotic or stool-transfer regimen.

stories.title: Ongoing gut symptoms
stories.lead: Follow mechanisms without forcing one microbial explanation.

steps.label: Describe the pattern
steps.text: Constipation, diarrhoea, pain and bloating can involve transit, fermentation, sensitivity and tissue inflammation. They are useful entrances into the atlas’s existing habitat research.

steps.label: Follow a process
steps.text: Transit time changes the resources available to microbes. Fermentation products and host responses create additional paths to examine in a specific symptom pattern.

steps.label: Recover function
steps.text: After an infection, symptoms can persist beyond pathogen clearance. Research that measures symptoms alongside microbial functions helps separate recovery of the person from a single stool readout.

stories.practical: Use the habitat links to explore the process behind a symptom. Persistent symptoms need an assessment that includes diet, medicines and non-microbial causes. Severe pain, blood in stool, unexplained weight loss or dehydration are reasons to seek medical care.

stories.title: Cholera
stories.lead: A toxin turns the small intestine into a route for rapid water loss.

steps.label: Contaminated water
steps.text: Cholera spreads through food or water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae. Safe water and sanitation interrupt the route into the gut.

steps.label: A toxin changes transport
steps.text: Toxigenic bacteria colonise the small intestine. Cholera toxin increases cellular cAMP, driving chloride secretion; water follows into the intestinal lumen.

steps.label: Water leaves the body
steps.text: Profuse watery diarrhoea can cause life-threatening dehydration within hours. The immediate problem is loss of water and salts.

steps.label: Replace what is lost
steps.text: Oral rehydration solution uses glucose–sodium absorption to bring water back into the body. Severe dehydration needs urgent medical care and intravenous fluids. Antibiotics are used for severe cases; vaccination and safe water help prevent infection.

stories.practical: Start oral rehydration promptly and seek urgent care for profuse watery diarrhoea or signs of dehydration. Use correctly prepared oral rehydration salts and safe water.

stories.title: Salmonellosis
stories.lead: Non-typhoidal Salmonella commonly causes diarrhoea, fever and abdominal cramps after contaminated food or contact.

steps.label: Exposure
steps.text: Non-typhoidal Salmonella reaches the intestine after contaminated food, water or animal contact. The organism must survive stomach acid before establishing itself at the intestinal surface.

steps.label: Cross the surface
steps.text: Salmonella uses secretion machinery to manipulate host cells and enter intestinal tissue. Epithelial and immune-cell sensing triggers an inflammatory response.

steps.label: Inflammation & competition
steps.text: Neutrophils enter the responding tissue, and fluid handling changes, producing diarrhoea and cramps. Inflammation also changes the microbial habitat, which Salmonella can exploit to compete with resident organisms.

steps.label: Recovery
steps.text: Replacing fluid losses is central. Antibiotics are reserved for severe infection and people at risk of invasive disease; they generally do not shorten uncomplicated illness in otherwise healthy people.
steps.schematic: Fluid replacement; treatment matched to severity

stories.practical: Replacing lost fluids is central. Antibiotics are reserved for particular patients or severe infection; dehydration, blood in stool or persistent fever require assessment.

stories.title: Campylobacter infection
stories.lead: Campylobacter infection is a common foodborne cause of diarrhoea and abdominal pain.

steps.label: Exposure
steps.text: Campylobacter commonly arrives through undercooked poultry, unpasteurised milk or contaminated water. Cross-contamination can move it from raw food onto ready-to-eat food.

steps.label: Mucus & epithelium
steps.text: Motile bacteria reach the mucus and epithelial surface. Attachment, invasion and bacterial products stimulate local inflammation. The mechanism differs from cholera’s predominantly secretory toxin effect.

steps.label: Inflammatory diarrhoea
steps.text: The inflamed lining produces abdominal pain, fever and diarrhoea that may be bloody. Immune activity is part of both controlling the infection and producing the symptoms.

steps.label: Recovery
steps.text: Most people recover without antibiotics. Replace fluid losses; severe disease or higher-risk patients may need antibiotics chosen with resistance in mind. Persistent neurological or joint symptoms after infection need assessment.

stories.practical: Most cases improve with supportive care. Severe illness or higher-risk patients may need antibiotics selected with local resistance in mind.

stories.title: Shigellosis
stories.lead: Shigella spreads readily by the faecal–oral route and can cause fever, cramps and bloody diarrhoea.

steps.label: Low-dose transmission
steps.text: Very small numbers of Shigella can establish infection. Faecal–oral spread through hands, close contact, food or water makes household and childcare transmission important.

steps.label: Enter colonic tissue
steps.text: Shigella crosses into the colonic lining, escapes into the inside of cells and can spread between neighbouring epithelial cells using host actin.

steps.label: Damage & dysentery
steps.text: Inflammation and epithelial injury produce frequent small stools, abdominal cramps and sometimes blood. Tissue invasion explains why this differs from a purely watery secretory diarrhoea.

steps.label: Interrupt transmission
steps.text: Fluids prevent dehydration. Many infections resolve without antibiotics; when antibiotics are needed, resistance testing matters. Avoid anti-diarrhoeal drugs such as loperamide when there is bloody diarrhoea.

stories.practical: Fluid replacement and infection control matter. Testing can help guide antibiotic treatment because resistance patterns vary and increasingly limit options.

stories.title: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection
stories.lead: STEC infection can cause severe abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea.

steps.label: Acquire a toxigenic strain
steps.text: Some E. coli strains carry genes for Shiga toxin. Exposure can come from contaminated produce, undercooked meat, unpasteurised products, water or contact with animals.
steps.schematic: Toxigenic E. coli reaches the colon

steps.label: Attachment & toxin
steps.text: Important STEC strains attach closely to intestinal epithelial cells and disrupt their absorptive surface. Shiga toxin inhibits protein synthesis in susceptible host cells.

steps.label: Beyond diarrhoea
steps.text: Bloody diarrhoea and severe cramps can be followed by haemolytic uraemic syndrome: red-cell destruction, low platelets and kidney injury. The toxin’s effects extend beyond the gut.

steps.label: Recognise the difference
steps.text: Prompt assessment and hydration matter. Antibiotics and anti-motility medicines can increase complications in STEC infection and should not be used as a generic response to bloody diarrhoea. Reduced urination is an urgent warning sign.
steps.schematic: Hydration + assessment; avoid harmful empiric treatment

stories.practical: Suspected infection needs clinical assessment and stool testing. Antibiotics and anti-diarrhoeal medicines can be inappropriate in STEC; hydration and monitoring for complications are important.

stories.title: Rotavirus gastroenteritis
stories.lead: Rotavirus causes vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly in young children, and can produce dangerous dehydration.

steps.label: Exposure
steps.text: Rotavirus spreads through faecal contamination of hands and surfaces. Young children are particularly vulnerable to severe dehydration during their first infections.

steps.label: Infect absorptive cells
steps.text: The virus infects mature absorptive cells on small-intestinal villi. Cell injury reduces absorption; viral proteins also alter intestinal secretion and signalling.

steps.label: Fluid loss
steps.text: Reduced absorption and increased secretion produce watery diarrhoea, often with vomiting and fever. A child can lose fluid faster than it is replaced.

steps.label: Replace & prevent
steps.text: Oral rehydration replaces water and salts; severe dehydration needs urgent care. Antibiotics do not treat rotavirus. Vaccination is a major preventive measure.

stories.practical: Oral rehydration is central, with urgent care for significant dehydration. Vaccination is an effective preventive measure according to the local childhood schedule.

stories.title: Cryptosporidiosis
stories.lead: Cryptosporidium is a protozoal parasite that causes watery diarrhoea, often after contaminated water or contact.

steps.label: Swallow oocysts
steps.text: Cryptosporidium oocysts spread through contaminated water, food, hands and animal contact. They tolerate chlorine levels normally used in pools, so routine chlorination alone does not remove the risk.

steps.label: Attach to the surface
steps.text: The parasite develops at the brush border of intestinal epithelial cells in a specialised compartment. It occupies and damages the absorptive surface.
steps.schematic: Parasite at the epithelial brush border

steps.label: Persistent watery diarrhoea
steps.text: Changes to absorption and secretion produce watery diarrhoea. Illness can be prolonged and especially severe in people with impaired immune function.
steps.schematic: Surface injury → poor absorption → fluid loss

steps.label: Recovery & prevention
steps.text: Replace fluid losses and seek care for prolonged illness or immune suppression. Treatment depends on age and immune status. Safe water and avoiding swimming while infectious help interrupt spread.

stories.practical: Treatment addresses dehydration, the parasite when indicated and immune status. Persistent or severe diarrhoea warrants assessment; water and hygiene measures reduce transmission.

stories.title: Amoebiasis
stories.lead: Entamoeba histolytica can cause colitis and bloody diarrhoea and sometimes spreads to the liver.

infection_diagram.exposure: Cysts in faecally contaminated food / water

steps.label: Swallow cysts
steps.text: Entamoeba histolytica is acquired by swallowing cysts. After excystation in the intestine, feeding forms called trophozoites can colonise the large bowel.

steps.label: Invade the lining
steps.text: Some infections remain within the lumen; invasive trophozoites adhere to and destroy colonic tissue. Ulceration can produce abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea.

steps.label: Reach the liver
steps.text: Organisms can enter portal blood and reach the liver, where an abscess may form. Fever and right-upper abdominal pain can therefore follow an infection whose entry point was intestinal.

steps.label: Treat both locations
steps.text: Diagnosis needs to distinguish E. histolytica from look-alike species. Invasive disease requires treatment of tissue infection followed by a medicine that clears organisms remaining in the intestinal lumen.

stories.practical: Diagnosis uses appropriate stool or other tests. Treatment targets invasive infection and organisms remaining in the bowel, with regimens chosen by a clinician.

stories.title: Ascariasis
stories.lead: Ascaris roundworms are acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil or food.

steps.label: Swallow mature eggs
steps.text: Ascaris eggs reach soil through faecal contamination and must develop there before becoming infectious. Ingestion on contaminated hands or food starts the human infection.

steps.label: Larval migration
steps.text: Larvae hatch, cross the intestinal wall and travel through the circulation to the lungs. They ascend the airways, are swallowed and return to the small intestine.

steps.label: Adult worms
steps.text: Adults live within the small-intestinal lumen. Heavy burdens can obstruct the intestine; wandering worms can enter the biliary tract. Eggs leave in stool and continue the environmental cycle.
steps.schematic: Adult worms in lumen → eggs in stool

steps.label: Clear & prevent reinfection
steps.text: Anthelmintic treatment clears the worms. Sanitation prevents eggs reaching soil; washing hands and produce reduces ingestion. Severe abdominal pain or signs of obstruction need urgent assessment.

stories.practical: Diagnosis and deworming address established infection. Sanitation and preventing soil contamination interrupt transmission; severe abdominal symptoms need assessment.

stories.title: Hookworm infection
stories.lead: Hookworm larvae usually enter through contaminated soil and develop into worms attached to the intestine.

steps.label: Larvae enter skin
steps.text: Infective larvae in contaminated soil commonly penetrate exposed skin. Footwear and sanitation act at this entry point. Some hookworm species can also be acquired by ingestion.

steps.label: Migrate to the intestine
steps.text: Larvae travel through circulation and the lungs, ascend the airway and are swallowed. They mature in the small intestine.

steps.label: Feed on blood
steps.text: Adult worms attach to the intestinal lining and feed on blood. Continued loss can deplete iron, connecting the infection directly to anaemia, fatigue and impaired growth.
steps.schematic: Attached worm → blood loss → iron depletion

steps.label: Repair the deficit
steps.text: Anthelmintic treatment removes the source of ongoing loss. Iron and nutritional recovery address what has already been depleted. Preventing soil contamination reduces repeated exposure.

stories.practical: Anthelmintic treatment and correction of iron deficiency address different parts of recovery. Footwear and sanitation reduce exposure in endemic settings.

stories.title: Whipworm infection
stories.lead: Trichuris whipworms infect the large intestine after eggs are swallowed.

infection_diagram.exposure: Swallowed mature eggs from contaminated soil

steps.label: Environmental eggs
steps.text: Whipworm eggs mature in contaminated soil. People acquire infection by swallowing infective eggs on hands or food.

steps.label: Embed in the colon
steps.text: Larvae hatch and develop into adults in the large intestine. The thin front end of the worm embeds in the mucosal lining.
steps.schematic: Adult worm embedded in colonic mucosa

steps.label: Heavy worm burden
steps.text: Light infection may cause few symptoms. Heavy burdens can produce abdominal pain, diarrhoea, blood loss, impaired growth and, in severe cases, rectal prolapse.

steps.label: Clear the burden
steps.text: Deworming and nutritional support address different parts of recovery. Sanitation and washing hands and produce reduce repeated ingestion of infective eggs.

stories.practical: Deworming and nutritional recovery are central. Safe sanitation and reducing soil contamination prevent repeated exposure.

stories.title: Strongyloidiasis
stories.lead: Strongyloides can maintain infection through an internal reinfection cycle for years.

steps.label: Entry & migration
steps.text: Strongyloides larvae penetrate skin exposed to contaminated soil, migrate through the body and reach the small intestine. Adult females live in the intestinal mucosa.

steps.label: An internal cycle
steps.text: Eggs hatch within the intestine. Some larvae develop into infective forms before leaving the host and penetrate intestinal or perianal tissue, creating autoinfection.

steps.label: Persistence & hyperinfection
steps.text: Autoinfection can maintain the parasite for decades without another environmental exposure. Corticosteroids and other immune suppression can accelerate the cycle into dangerous hyperinfection and dissemination.
steps.schematic: Autoinfection loop accelerates under immune suppression

steps.label: Find & clear infection
steps.text: Exposure history and appropriate testing matter before immunosuppression in at-risk people. Ivermectin is central to treatment; severe infection requires urgent specialist management.

stories.practical: Exposure history and appropriate testing matter before immunosuppression in at-risk people. Ivermectin-based treatment is prescribed for confirmed or clinically relevant infection.

stories.title: Pinworm infection
stories.lead: Pinworms commonly affect children and households, causing night-time itching around the anus.

steps.label: Swallow eggs
steps.text: Pinworm eggs spread on hands, under fingernails, bedding and household surfaces. Swallowing eggs starts the intestinal cycle.

steps.label: Mature in the bowel
steps.text: Larvae hatch in the small intestine. Adults establish themselves mainly in the caecum and adjacent large bowel.
steps.schematic: Egg → larva → adult in large bowel

steps.label: Night-time egg laying
steps.text: Female worms migrate to perianal skin to lay eggs, often at night. Itching encourages scratching, transferring eggs to fingers and allowing reinfection or household spread.

steps.label: Break household spread
steps.text: Treatment commonly involves a repeat dose and coordinated household measures. Handwashing, short nails and washing bedding interrupt egg transfer; care should follow local age and pregnancy guidance.

stories.practical: Treatment often addresses household transmission as well as the infected person. Handwashing, short nails and washing bedding help reduce reinfection.

stories.title: Hepatitis A
stories.lead: Hepatitis A is a liver infection spread through contaminated food, water or close contact.

steps.label: Enteric exposure
steps.text: Hepatitis A spreads when virus from faecal contamination is swallowed. Food, water and close contact can carry the virus into the digestive tract.

steps.label: The liver is the target
steps.text: After enteric acquisition, the virus reaches the liver. Hepatocytes are the main site of replication, and the immune response contributes to liver injury.

steps.label: Return through bile
steps.text: Virus is shed into bile and then stool, allowing transmission before or during illness. Liver dysfunction can cause jaundice and dark urine. Hepatitis A does not establish chronic infection.

steps.label: Support & prevent
steps.text: Care is supportive, with assessment for dehydration or severe liver disease. Vaccination prevents infection; prompt post-exposure vaccination or immunoglobulin is used when indicated.

stories.practical: Supportive care and monitoring address illness. Vaccination and post-exposure measures prevent infection in relevant settings; severe vomiting or worsening jaundice needs assessment.

stories.title: Typhoid fever
stories.lead: Typhoid is a systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, usually acquired through contaminated food or water.

infection_diagram.exposure: Human faecal contamination of food / water

steps.label: Enter through the gut
steps.text: Salmonella Typhi is acquired from contaminated food or water. Humans are its reservoir, so sanitation and carrier detection are central to transmission.

steps.label: Cross into the body
steps.text: Bacteria cross the intestinal surface and survive within phagocytic cells. They spread beyond the gut, producing systemic infection rather than only local gastroenteritis.

steps.label: Persistence & shedding
steps.text: Systemic spread causes prolonged fever and illness. The gallbladder can support persistent carriage, with organisms returning through bile to the intestine and stool.

steps.label: Treat resistance-aware
steps.text: Effective antibiotics are essential and must reflect resistance patterns and travel history. Vaccination, safe water and sanitation reduce acquisition and onward spread.

stories.practical: Diagnosis and effective antibiotics are essential. The regimen depends on local resistance and travel history; vaccination and safe water reduce risk.

stories.title: Oral thrush
stories.lead: Oral thrush is overgrowth of Candida in the mouth, producing white patches or soreness.

infection_diagram.exposure: Resident yeast expands in altered oral conditions

steps.label: A resident organism
steps.text: Candida can be present in the mouth without causing illness. Antibiotics, dentures, inhaled steroids, immune suppression and metabolic conditions can change the local environment.

steps.label: Growth on the surface
steps.text: Yeast growth and filament formation support attachment and biofilm formation on oral surfaces. Visible plaques can develop on mucosal tissue.

steps.label: Local symptoms
steps.text: Oral candidiasis can produce white patches, soreness and altered taste. This is a disease of the mouth; it does not by itself demonstrate an intestinal Candida infection.

steps.label: Treat the habitat too
steps.text: Antifungal treatment addresses the infection. Denture hygiene, mouth rinsing after inhaled steroids and assessment of recurrent episodes address contributing conditions.

stories.practical: Care addresses the local infection and contributing factors, with antifungal treatment when needed. Recurrent episodes can prompt assessment of medicines or underlying conditions.

stories.title: Periodontitis
stories.lead: Periodontitis is inflammatory destruction of tissues supporting the teeth.

infection_diagram.exposure: Persistent biofilm at the gum margin

steps.label: A biofilm at the tooth
steps.text: Oral bacteria attach to a stable tooth surface and form plaque. Around the gum margin, that community is in direct contact with host tissue and its inflammatory response.

steps.label: An inflamed pocket
steps.text: Inflammation and periodontal pocket formation alter oxygen, nutrients and access to tissue-derived material. The changed habitat supports a different microbial community.

steps.label: Supporting tissue is lost
steps.text: Periodontitis destroys connective attachment and alveolar bone supporting the tooth. The mechanism combines a biofilm with host-mediated tissue damage.

steps.label: Disrupt the biofilm
steps.text: Professional periodontal treatment and ongoing plaque control act on the local cause. Smoking and diabetes affect healing. This local mechanism is why oral ecology belongs in a digestive atlas.

stories.practical: Professional periodontal treatment and sustained daily plaque control are central. Smoking, diabetes and other contributing factors affect disease and healing.

stories.title: Dental caries
stories.lead: Dental caries develops when repeated acid production in dental plaque causes mineral loss from teeth.

steps.label: A retained community
steps.text: Dental plaque retains microbes on tooth surfaces. Saliva, food exposure and cleaning shape this habitat. Caries is a community-and-chemistry process, not simply the presence of one organism.

steps.label: Sugar becomes acid
steps.text: Plaque microbes ferment available carbohydrate into organic acids. Local pH falls, favouring acid-tolerant organisms when exposures are frequent.

steps.label: Mineral balance shifts
steps.text: Acid dissolves tooth mineral. Saliva and fluoride support remineralisation, but repeated acid exposure can make net mineral loss accumulate into a cavity.
steps.schematic: Repeated low pH → enamel mineral loss

steps.label: Change the balance
steps.text: Fluoride, plaque control and reducing frequent sugar exposure support prevention. Established lesions need dental assessment and treatment matched to their stage.

stories.practical: Fluoride, effective cleaning, sugar-exposure patterns and dental treatment address different stages. Pain, swelling or a dental abscess need prompt care.

stories.title: Gingivitis
stories.lead: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums, often causing bleeding with cleaning.

infection_diagram.exposure: Plaque accumulation at the gum margin

steps.label: Plaque accumulates
steps.text: A biofilm builds up where tooth and gum meet. Changes in cleaning and local plaque retention increase contact between the community and the gum tissue.

steps.label: Gum immune response
steps.text: Microbial products stimulate local immune cells and blood vessels. Increased blood flow and immune-cell recruitment produce swollen, red gums.

steps.label: Bleeding with cleaning
steps.text: Inflamed tissue bleeds more easily. Gingivitis is distinguished from periodontitis by the absence of the supporting attachment and bone loss that defines periodontitis.

steps.label: Remove the stimulus
steps.text: Effective daily cleaning and professional plaque removal can reverse plaque-induced gingivitis. Persistent bleeding needs dental assessment, including checking for periodontitis.

stories.practical: Daily plaque control and professional cleaning support recovery. Persistent bleeding should be checked for periodontal disease and other contributors.

function:Fermentation.title: Food, partnerships and fermentation
paragraphs: Specialist bacteria open complex carbohydrates to their neighbours. Cross-feeding experiments connect released sugars, acetate and butyrate production. Human dietary interventions then test changes in the community and immune measurements.

The fermented-food and high-fibre arms of the Stanford trial produced different responses: diversity rose in the fermented-food arm, while microbial carbohydrate-processing capacity increased with fibre.
function:Fermentation.author: Gut Atlas seed

entity:movement.title: Movement and microbial response
paragraphs: Six weeks of endurance exercise changed microbial metabolism in lean participants, with changes that largely reversed after training stopped. A shorter interval-training study improved fitness without a detectable shift in community composition.
Together these studies make duration, baseline physiology and metabolic function useful variables to investigate.
entity:movement.author: Gut Atlas seed

taxon:Helicobacter.title: A bacterium in the gastric environment
paragraphs: Urea transport and urease help H. pylori manage gastric acidity. Changes in mucus properties help explain how the bacterium reaches the lining. Long-term eradication trials connect treatment to reduced gastric cancer incidence.
taxon:Helicobacter.author: Gut Atlas seed

topic:gut-brain.title: From microbial signals to human experience
paragraphs: Human cohort research links microbial functions with quality of life and depression. A small intervention with B. longum 1714 measured stress and memory responses in healthy volunteers. These designs examine different parts of the same biological conversation.
topic:gut-brain.author: Gut Atlas seed

topic:pain.title: Gut microbiome, cytokines and persistent pain
paragraphs: Start with the Sima matched pilot, then compare non-surgical pain with surgical outcomes and structural spine disease. These cohorts do not share one universal diversity pattern or bacterial signature.

Follow the cytokines separately: the inflammatory-biomarker synthesis and Th17 study measured immune signals in back disorders. The mouse TNF experiments test microbiota–inflammation feedback, rather than human back-pain treatment.
topic:pain.author: Gut Atlas editorial
